etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English warm, werm, from Old English wearm, from Proto-West Germanic *warm, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, with different proposed origins:

definitions.definition: Of a somewhat high temperature.

quote.citation: 1863, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, The Herons of Elmwood:
quote.text: Warm and still is the summer night.

quote.citation: 1985, Robert Ferro, Blue Star:
quote.text: It seemed I was too excited for sleep, too warm, too young.

definitions.definition: Friendly and with affection.
Having a color in the part of the visible electromagnetic spectrum between red and yellow-green.
(informal) Close to a goal or correct answer.

quote.citation: 1876, William Black, “An Encounter”, in Madcap Violet. […], volume III, London: Macmillan and Co., →OCLC, page 74:
quote.text: That was a further clue; and here, indeed, young Mr. Dowse was getting "warm," as children say at blind-man's-buff, although, as a matter-of-fact, she had now been talking of George Miller at all.

definitions.definition: Fresh, of a scent; still able to be traced.
(figurative) Communicating a sense of comfort, ease, or pleasantness.
(archaic) Ardent, zealous.

quote.citation: 1646 (indicated as 1645), John Milton, “Song on May Morning”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Mirth, and youth, and warm desire!

quote.citation: 1712 September 22 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “THURSDAY, September 11, 1712”, in The Spectator, number 481; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume V, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: They say he's a warm man and does not care to be made mouths at.The spelling has been modernized.

quote.citation: 1776–1788, Edward Gibbon, chapter I, in The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:  […]  W[illiam] Strahan; and T[homas] Cadell, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: To the strength and fierceness of barbarians they added a contempt for life, which was derived from a warm persuasion of the immortality and transmigration of the soul.

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: I had been none of the warmest of partisans.

definitions.definition: (archaic, informal) Well off as to property, or in good circumstances; prosperous.

quote.citation: 1766, [Oliver Goldsmith], The Vicar of Wakefield: […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), Salisbury, Wiltshire:  […]  B. Collins, for F[rancis] Newbery, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: You shall have a draught upon him, payable at sight: and let me tell you he is as warm a man as any within five miles round him.

quote.citation: 1791, Charlotte Smith, Celestina, Broadview, published 2004, page 258:
quote.text: Mrs. and the Miss Cathcarts began to be considered as people of some consequence in the circle in which they moved, while he gradually obtained in the city the name of a warm man.

quote.citation: 1824, Geoffrey Crayon [pseudonym; Washington Irving], Tales of a Traveller, (please specify |part=1 to 4), Philadelphia, Pa.: H[enry] C[harles] Carey & I[saac] Lea, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I know the Stuyvesant family —puff— every one of them —puff— not a more respectable family in the province —puff— old standards —puff— warm householders —puff— none of your upstarts

definitions.definition: (archaic) Requiring arduous effort.

quote.citation: 1929, The Listener, numbers 41-50, page 552:
quote.text: The circular iron platform over there is used in the task of tyring the wheels, a warm job, too, by the way.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make or keep warm.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 44 44-Chapter-15/# 15::
quote.text: Then shall it [an ash tree] be for a man to burn; for he will take thereof and warm himself.

quote.citation: 1825, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Morituri Salutamus:
quote.text: enough to warm, but not enough to burn

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become warm, to heat up.
(intransitive) (sometimes in the form warm up) To favour increasingly. [with to]

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 5, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: Mr. Campion appeared suitably impressed and she warmed to him. He was very easy to talk to with those long clown lines in his pale face, a natural goon, born rather too early she suspected.

definitions.definition: (ditransitive with to) To cause (someone) to favour (something) increasingly.

quote.citation: 2006, Matt Wray, Not Quite White, page xi:
quote.text: It is with no small degree of irony that I confess that immersing myself in an interdisciplinary project has warmed me to the seductions of disciplinary perspectives.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become ardent or animated.
(transitive) To make engaged or earnest; to interest; to engage; to excite ardor or zeal in; to enliven.

quote.citation: 1717 November 20, Alexander Pope, letter to the Bishop of Rochester
quote.text: there was a collection of all that had been written […] : I warmed my head with them.

quote.citation: 1827, [John Keble], The Christian Year: Thoughts in Verse for the Sundays and Holydays throughout the Year, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  [B]y W. Baxter, for J. Parker; and C[harles] and J[ohn] Rivington, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Bright hopes, that erst the bosom warmed.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give emotional warmth to a person.

quote.citation: 1886, Joseph Augustus Seiss, Right Life: Or, Candid Talks On Vital Themes:
quote.text: That is just the way God tells me this book is His Word. I read it, and it warms me and gives me light.

definitions.definition: (transitive, colloquial) To beat or spank.

quote.citation: 1945, The Atlantic, volume 176, page 94:
quote.text: Not bothering to turn around and not missing a mouthful, Myrtle comforted her with threats of "I'll warm your bottom"; "I'll turn you over to your dad"; "I'll lock you in the truck"; "I'll send for the bogey man" — all of which Darleen ignored  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, colloquial) To scold or abuse verbally.
(computing, transitive) To prepopulate (a cache) so that its contents are ready for other users.
(colloquial) The act of warming, or the state of being warmed; a heating.

quote.citation: 1843 December 19, Charles Dickens, “(please specify the page number)”, in A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas, London: Chapman & Hall, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Sit ye down before the fire , my dear , and have a warm
